newsitem.title: INDIA: Lack of clear policy could hit India power targets.
newsitem.headline: Lack of clear policy could hit India power targets.

text.p: Private power producers said on Thursday that India's ability to meet its power targets might be jeopardised if it failed to formulate a power policy and identify risks.
"We don't have any policy on the power sector," said Harry Dhaul, director general of the Independent Power Producers Association of India (IPPAI).
Private investors have so far pumped about 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion) into the power sector but the government estimates the country needs another $79 billion to ease acute shortages.
India added only 14,799 megawatts of power generation capacity between 1992 and 1995, well below the target of 30,858 megawatts for the five-year period ending in 1996.
With an installed capacity of 87,000 megawatts per year, India will need an additional 142,000 megawatts by 2007, according to industry estimates.
In February, following a presidential decree, an expert committee was set up to work out a framework for private investment in power transmission, but parliament has yet to pass laws, Dhaul said.
Dhaul said the government needed to take steps to ensure power generation targets were fulfilled, and consult private power producers before framing a policy on the sector.
"The distribution and transmission of the power need to be privatised," he said.
Dhaul said most of the country's proposed power projects might be scrapped if risks were not properly identified.
"Risks need to be identified, shared, mitigated, addressed and negotiated if any substantial measure or success is to be expected in the private power development," the IPPAI said in a statement.
Dhaul said a lack of long-term foreign exchange availability and arbitrary allocations might endanger the survival of nearly 15,000 megawatts of liquid fuel-based power projects in the pipeline.
He said a plethora of public interest litigations also hampered power projects.
"The companies may not be able to achieve financial closure if there are undue delays or litigation," Dhaul said.
He also stressed the need for assessing the creditworthiness of the buyer before entering into an agreement.
"Most of the state electricity boards are not in a position to buy the high priced power from private producers and might not be able to meet their commitment," Dhaul added.
India opened up its power sector under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.
U.S. firms Enron Corp and CMS Energy Corp have been front-runners among foreign power generation firms. -- New Delhi newsroom +91-11 301 2024
